title: Bouillabaisse
subtitle: Provençal fish stew with rouille
excerpt: The great fish stew of Marseille: a saffron-scented broth built on a base of fennel, tomato, and white wine, with mixed whole fish and shellfish cooked directly in it. Served with rouille on toasted bread.
sourceNotes: Bouillabaisse is a dish of Provence with origins in the fishing communities of Marseille; described in detail in Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), and Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The broth base can be made a day ahead. Add the fish on the day and cook for 15 minutes before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Provençal sauce of olive oil, garlic, saffron, and chilli pepper, thickened with breadcrumbs or egg yolk. Traditionally served with bouillabaisse spread on croutons and floated in the broth.

content.text: Bouillabaisse begins as a fisherman's dish: whatever came up in the net that morning went into the pot. The bones of bony, gelatinous fish give the broth its body; the cooking method (boil-then-simmer, which is what the name describes) is the technique that makes it distinct. For a home version, use a mix of firm white fish, mussels, and prawns.

attrs.title: The fish
attrs.body: Classic bouillabaisse uses firm Mediterranean fish: rascasse, grondin, John Dory, monkfish. For a home version, use 800 g of firm white fish (monkfish, John Dory, or gurnard) cut into large pieces, plus 300 g mussels and 8 large prawns. Oily fish such as salmon or mackerel are not suitable.

items.prepNote: or firm white fish, cut into 4 cm pieces
one tin chopped or 4 fresh, roughly chopped
or water with a fish stock cube
a strip of peel, no pith
for rouille: mix with 2 crushed garlic cloves, a pinch of saffron, and a pinch of cayenne

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the fennel and onion. Cook for 10 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, wine, thyme, bay leaves, orange peel, and chilli flakes. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes break down.
Pour in the stock and add the saffron water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 20 minutes. Taste for salt. Remove the herb sprigs, bay leaves, and orange peel.

Bring the broth to a vigorous boil. Add the firmest fish pieces first (monkfish). Boil hard for 3 minutes, then add the prawns and mussels. Continue at a strong simmer for 5 more minutes, until the mussels have opened and the fish is cooked through. Discard any mussels that have not opened.
Mix the mayonnaise with 2 crushed garlic cloves, a pinch of saffron-steeped water, and cayenne to taste. This is a quick rouille.
Ladle the broth into wide bowls and distribute the fish. Float a toasted crouton smeared with rouille on top. Pass more rouille and croutons alongside.

items.symptom: The broth is thin and watery
items.cause: Not enough vegetables or not cooked long enough
items.fix: Simmer the broth for an extra 10 minutes before adding the fish. Some cooks strain and reduce the broth slightly at this point.

items.symptom: The fish is overcooked and breaking apart
items.cause: Cooked too long or too gently
items.fix: The vigorous boil is important. Fish cooks quickly; add firmest pieces first and time carefully.
Discard any that remain closed after cooking. Do not force them.

items.cause: Too little saffron or not steeped properly
items.fix: Steep the saffron in hot water for at least 10 minutes; it releases more colour with time.

content.text: The people of Marseille are very particular about what qualifies as a real bouillabaisse. In 1980 a group of Marseillais restaurateurs published a charter listing the minimum requirements: at least four of the traditional rock fish must be present, served in two courses (broth first, then fish), with rouille and toasted bread. The home version loosens these constraints while keeping the essential character: a fragrant saffron and fennel broth, high heat, mixed seafood.
